parsed.explanation: The combined regime is driven by federal entry and custody exposure. A trans visitor's foreign passport or visa can be questioned under the binary-sex policy; discrepancy may lead to refusal, secondary screening, or a permanent fraud finding, and entry-related detention is federal immigration custody with documented forced labour, beatings and sexual abuse. The division's sanctuary care law, protective-law band, identity-based state prison placement and surgery funding are real mitigations after entry, but they do not govern the border, federal facilities, federal threat framing or federal custody. State-level facility bans are not documented locally, though national government-funded facilities are restricted. Street-violence figures are raw counts without denominators and cannot establish elevated individual risk. Litigation and enjoined orders create uncertainty, not safety. The result is High Risk: worse than exclusion-only because of lifetime-ban and abusive-custody exposure, but above extreme criminalisation because the division is protective and no execution or general criminalisation of identity is documented.

entry_documents.exposure: National binary-sex policy; X/new marker processing stopped; screening cable requires refusal or additional evidence on discrepancy or reasonable doubt; suspected misrepresentation can support permanent fraud ineligibility; reports of passports confiscated or blocked and foreign advisories.
entry_documents.protection: Existing X passports remain valid until expiry; fraud finding is not automatic and requires four elements with limited waiver; policy is under legal challenge; legal-aid FAQ exists.
entry_documents.interaction: Foreign passport or visa mismatch can trigger secondary screening and refusal before any state sanctuary attaches; state protections cannot cure a federal border finding.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: Immigration custody reports forced labour, beatings, solitary confinement and severe sexual abuse of trans men; national corrections conversion-therapy policies include haircutting and hormone removal; trans-prisoner reporting stopped.
investigation_detention_custody.protection: Division state prison policy documented identity-based housing and gender-affirming surgery funding in 2015; housing last confirmed 2021; no trans-only facility documented.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: Entry-related detention is federal, where documented abuse sits; state corrections protections apply only in state custody and are unconfirmed after 2021.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: National executive order bars trans people from government-funded single-sex facilities matching identity; many states ban facilities, four criminalise some bathroom use, and a trans student was arrested under one.
federal_state_facilities.protection: Division is in the protective-law band and no local facility ban is documented; national hate-crime and partial anti-discrimination coverage exist.
federal_state_facilities.interaction: Federal facilities and other states' bans remain operative; division protections do not govern federal buildings or cross-state travel.

care_services.exposure: National orders label minor gender-affirming care mutilation, freeze funding, threaten school staff, subpoena hospital records and propose an insurance bar; immigration custody denied care.
care_services.protection: Division sanctuary law lets out-of-state youth obtain hormones and blockers and shields families from state child-abuse investigation or prosecution; state prison surgery funding.
care_services.interaction: State shield protects families seeking care inside the division, but federal funding, insurance, investigative and custody rules still reach the journey; adult routine care is not clearly barred.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: Counterterrorism strategy prioritises 'radically pro-transgender' violent groups; DOJ reward guidance references 'radical gender ideology'; school-prosecution order; official hostility.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: National hate-crime statute covers gender identity; 22 states plus the capital outlaw gender-identity discrimination; division has protective laws.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: Federal threat framing can prompt investigation or surveillance regardless of state protection; state law cannot cancel federal enforcement.

minors_guardians.exposure: National order defines care for minors as mutilation and directs investigations, prosecutions of teachers and funding cuts; proposed insurance bar; a minor's document mismatch at the border can trigger screening; guardians may face inquiry in hostile states.
minors_guardians.protection: Division sanctuary expressly shields families travelling for care from state child-abuse investigations or prosecution; youth can access hormones and blockers.
minors_guardians.interaction: Families gain real state protection inside the division, but federal border, funding, insurance and threat-framing exposures remain; provider and teacher liability is unsettled.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: Division recorded 198 anti-LGBTQ incidents in 2025, the highest raw count; its largest city saw a rise in hate-crime reports; the source gives no population denominator, so individual risk is not established.
street_violence_police_response.protection: National gender-identity hate-crime statute; division protective-law band; July 2026 analysis calls it low recorded-incident and safest-laws band; police response is undocumented.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: The raw count cannot outweigh the protective-law and no-denominator caveat; recourse exists on paper but local police response to trans visitors is not documented.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: Passport policy, executive orders and health rules are in litigation; some measures are blocked or enjoined; fraud ineligibility and custody practices remain operative risks; prison housing is unconfirmed after 2021; incident methodology is unreported.
remedies_unknowns.protection: Courts have enjoined several orders; legal-aid FAQ; state sanctuary and protective statutes; national hate-crime law.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: Remedies are slow and federal; they do not guarantee entry or release; state remedies cannot bind federal border or custody actors.

anchor_checks.comparison: 0.15-A is markedly worse: gender presentation itself is criminalised as deception, arrest is routine, capital prosecution is concrete, and custody harm is lethal with illusory remedies. Here the documented severe harms sit in federal immigration custody and a possible lifetime fraud finding, not in a general presentation offence, and the division adds sanctuary and protective prison and care rules. The case remains far above 0.15-A, but not safe.

0.35-A has routine border exclusion for transgender visitors, no effective remedy, and no imprisonment. This dossier is similar at the border—discretionary refusal and humiliating screening—but worse because suspected misrepresentation can support permanent ineligibility and entry custody carries documented abuse. It is better after entry, since the division has sanctuary care, protective-law band and identity-based state prison placement. Net: roughly the same high-risk tier, slightly below 0.35-A.

0.55-B involves extended secondary screening, luggage searches, missed connections and administrative refusal without criminal prosecution. This dossier is more severe: it adds a possible lifetime fraud finding, documented abusive federal immigration custody, national facilities restrictions and counterterrorism threat-framing. The division's protections mitigate daily life after entry but do not reach the border or federal custody, so the case sits below 0.55-B.

0.85-B has recognised nonbinary passports, specialist border training, body cameras, legal aid and tribunal-ordered release. This dossier has restricted passport and visa markers, suspicion-based screening, possible permanent fraud ineligibility and documented federal custody abuse. The division's sanctuary and protective laws provide partial mitigation, but they cannot offset federal entry and custody rules. The case is far below 0.85-B.

parsed.synthesis: In practice the visitor meets the harshest rules first: federal document screening and possible fraud ineligibility, then federal immigration custody if refused or detained. Only after admission does the division's sanctuary and protective-law regime operate, and it cannot bind federal actors. State prison identity-based housing is a genuine protection in state custody, but its 2021 confirmation is stale and it does not reach federal detention. The care shield helps travelling families inside the division, yet federal funding, insurance and threat-framing rules remain. Local facility bans are not documented, but nearby states' bans and federal facility restrictions make cross-state movement risky. Raw anti-LGBTQ incident counts lack denominators, so they cannot be weighed as elevated per-visitor risk.
